full_text:
Interviewer:	I'll start by telling you a bit about what we're doing. The project that we're working on is mainly looking at engineering students but we wanted to included design students as well. The reason we're looking at engineering is because it is male dominated but we think the design is quite male dominated as well and also because we're working with another university and there design & technology comes under engineering, therefore we decided to include it under our remit as well. We're looking at women's early experiences of work, their higher education and why they decided to do an industrial placement, things like that. OK, if I start off asking you just a few background questions about how you decided to choose this degree and things like that. It is the design and technology course that you're doing?

Subject:	Yeah, industrial design & technology.

Interviewer:	What 'A' levels did you do?

Subject:	I did design technology, graphics and French and maths.

Interviewer:	OK, what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	All girls Grammar.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

Subject:	Yeah, in year 11 for my work experience I worked for 2 weeks in the design department of a shoe company for children's footwear.

Interviewer:	OK, do either of your parents work in the industry?

Subject:	My mum used to do interior designing erm freelance, and she did lots of text – she did a textile degree and my dad does fashion – but it's selling.

Interviewer:	OK. When and why then do you think that you decided to do design technology?

Subject:	Erm, I always liked arty things, from my mum, and then at school I found – I mean I was an all rounder but I always enjoyed art and design technology and then it was just one of my best subjects at GCSE which I really – I really enjoyed it at GCSE so I did it for A level and then it was just the obvious choice really.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that the fact that your mum is involved in the industry has influenced you at all?

Subject:	Erm, I think it gave me an interest in it, but it was just the fact that I enjoy it and that I'm good at it, that made me choose it really.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Did you have any careers advice or anything like that?

Subject:	We had Careers Advice at school but I don't think it was that helpful. But I mean it always came up as one of the options that erm I was suited to. You know we went on computer programmes and spoke to advisors.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think it is that appeals to you about the subject?

Subject:	The subject I'm doing here is so broad, compared to other degrees. You get to do engineering subjects like mechanics and electronics but you get to do – you get to be creative, but you also get to make things as well, which you don't – you don't in many other things so – it's just so broad and varied. I think it's a lot more exciting than sitting, just listening to lots of lectures.

Interviewer:	OK, did you ever consider doing any other subjects?

Subject:	Erm, I considered doing something more engineering based but I thought that I'd miss the graphics side of it (yes) and I also considered doing the same course but with a language on the side, like French because I did that at A level, but now I'm just doing that on the side here rather than as part of my degree.

Interviewer:	OK, how did you decide to come to [this] University?

Subject:	Well, I came to the open day, with some friends, and I hadn't expected – I didn't realise they did my subject – well this subject here. So, I went to the product design area – they – the people there – told me that what I wanted to do sounded more like industrial design, which is slightly more creative. So I went on a department tour and picked up the syllabus and it just really appealed to me. It was my favourite course out of all the universities.

Interviewer:	OK, did you always want to do a sandwich course or did you just like the course and it happened to have…?

Subject:	No, I didn't. I only changed to that this September (OK). At first I was a bit too scared to go out into industry, in the middle of my degree. I'm still a bit scared I think – it will be really strange but, after advice from my parents I decided to go for it, because I just thought that it adds to your degree and I've been told that you get better marks in the final year, generally and also it will just – in my field you always need a minimum of 1 year's experience, and it'll be an easy way to get that.

Interviewer:	OK, when you decided that you wanted to do design & technology, did you realise it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Yes. I mean I – I was in an all girls school but there were only 6 of us in the whole school who did it at A level and when I went on open days I noticed I was usually one of the only girls. I think here there's more girls than I expected to be. When I went to [name] and some other universities, I saw hardly any other – it was a bit intimidating as well. I was quite scared, especially coming from an all girls environment to suddenly almost the opposite.

Interviewer:	Do you think that being in an all girls school affected your choice of subjects at all? Do you think you were encouraged more to do maths or science type subjects?

Subject:	You're encouraged more to do maths and science and IT but – and they weren't going to run design technology for my 'A' levels – for our year, but we did a petition and – I mean I was going to swap schools if they didn't provide it for me because I'd decided that's what I wanted to do. But, it did make me want to be more academic in my choices in general.

Interviewer:	Ok. Does it ever bother you that there aren't many women on the course?

Subject:	Erm, kind of. It's more the fact that it was quite intimidating and I felt – just things like men in the workshops woodwork and things, I just felt as though I would have less background in it because I know it's a stereotypical kind of view that, you know, boys will do that outside of school and I just thought that I'd be further behind and I think boys in general tend to be a lot more confident about their work and it's something that you need to be confident of your own ideas. But I mean, after the first – after the first few months, I realised that I was just on the same level as everyone else really – fine.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged to do this sort of subject?

Subject:	Yeah. I mean I think the fact that it's male dominated puts off a lot of people because it is quite intimidating and yeah and you kind of – if you don't – I don't know – you might think that you're less likely to get a job in the field, just because it's so male dominated and that people have ideas, even before they meet you because they know you're female. But what I've found is that it's not really the case – well so far.

Interviewer:	OK. What do you think could be done to encourage more women to the industry?

Subject:	Well, in school – being an all girls' school, it was really – the whole department was not on a level with everything else and I thought a lot of people were put off then. I mean I don't know if they're running A level design technology any more and it's quite disappointing and as I say a lot of people would be really good at it and would really enjoy it. So if they're not getting the chance. So it would be back in school I think.

Interviewer:	Do you think that people maybe don't choose to do it because they don't really know what it is about in the first place?

Subject:	Yeah and also – well, in my case, the GCSE was so much work compared to other subjects. A lot of – finding time to fit it in, which I mean – it's like now, you've still got to put a lot of extra time in and that puts people off 'cos they just think it's gonna take up a lot more time than everything else.

Interviewer:	OK, what characteristics do you think make a good designer?

Subject:	That's hard. Erm, good imagination and confidence in their ideas. You need to be able to communicate your ideas well and verbally and visually. You need to have a good background knowledge of materials and processes, so you know that the product's made and basic mechanics and electronics – so you know a bit of the idea, if possible. I think just erm people usually think it's people here who are more creative, who can draw but it's not just that. It's the ideas we have and how viable they are.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of those characteristics are more male or more female? I know you said earlier males are probably more confident.

Subject:	Yeah, I think in general they're a lot more confident when they explain their ideas and show them, whereas when we have girls in the class, they'll explain it but they'll point out the bad bits or they'll apologise and in general the guys don't do that and er the – I think a lot of the girls tend to be neater with their work, rather than just, you know, drawing it and sharing – but on the other hand there's things that girls have, like we keep getting told that females have better appreciation of colour and they're more sensitive to things like shapes and things – which is also useful. I think it's just mainly the confidence thing – the guys tend to be a lot more confident than the girls in their work, and it shows.

Interviewer:	Yes, OK. Do you think that there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in the industry?

Subject:	Er, I think the disadvantage is that in the kind of minority, and people might be put off just because they know – they know so many designers who are good and they're all male. Yeah. But, on the other hand I think it's good to have another point of view, another perspective on things and it's – you know – a slightly different energy in the team – yeah, and maybe a different outlook and different approach, which is more positive.

Interviewer:	OK. Has the course been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Erm, I think so, yeah. I think a lot of people have been surprised and we do have – I think it's a high drop out rate at the beginning, just because the work load is huge compared to well courses like geography, things like that. But, er yeah – it's yeah, it's quite – it's varied and that was what I was looking for.

Interviewer:	So were you surprised then at the amount of engineering and technical stuff that there was in it, or were you expecting that?

Subject:	No, I was hoping it would have as much as it did, last year because I didn't want to kind of lose my knowledge that I'd gained in my A levels, and I still wanted something academic in there, rather than just drawing all day (yes) you know workshop stuff – I wanted to think as well. But I mean I did find some of it quite hard, but they taught it from a basic level, which was quite good so were all on a level with each other by the end of year.

Interviewer:	OK, did it surprise you that your department is situated in the faculty of social sciences and not say engineering?

Subject:	I never remember which faculty you're in because I know the course is basically half engineering and half art but I mean they've just – there's a lot of engineering content in it, especially in first year. I mean we're in – we had to walk to the other side of the campus every single day. It belongs a lot more there I think, I mean I don't think – the other subjects that are in social science I think, apart from ergonomics they don't really overlap at all. So…

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think has been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Hmm, the worst things are the amount of work but then we were told to expect that and the fact that it's a lot of course work, so we have a lot of deadlines in, at the same time, and it's – you don't get much sleep at all. And it – a lot of the work is very time consuming. You can't just – the fact that you – you never actually hand it all in and have no work to do because there's always an on-going project. But then, I suppose that's something that I like anyway. Erm, and the best thing – hmm, I think our department in general, because we have a lot more seminars and workshops. I like the fact that we're a lot more bonded than other courses. We know everyone in the year and we see each other – we can chat during lesson time – it's like school, you can just sit there and work and talk to each other and I really like that.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think that the number of hours that you have to do will help you when you go to work in the industry because you'll be used to putting in more hours and having more structured?

Subject:	Yeah, I mean it's gonna help with me – with my organisation and, at the end of the day, I think I'll be getting a lot more out of my university degree than other people – if you know what – I have a lot more teaching hours so I'm gaining a lot more from the lectures than 3 hours a week.

Interviewer:	OK, are you pleased that you decided to do this course?

Subject:	Er, yes – still. I've had moments where I've just been overwhelmed by the amount of work, but other than that I do really enjoy it and it is what I want to carry on doing.

Interviewer:	OK. Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	Yes, erm there aren't as many female lecturers. We had one, Dina, but she's left now. And we had another – visiting lecturer she came in and talked about colour – did some colour workshops. I never really thought about that before. When we go up to engineering we've had female lecturers for materials – other than that they're just mainly male.

Interviewer:	Erm, have you noticed whether the female and male lecturers have got a different teaching style or whether they teach different types of subjects or anything like that.

Subject:	Er, within the department the female teacher – oh we have actually got a couple but I haven't really been taught by them – she was – she focussed a lot more on the emotional side, compared to some of the male lecturers but I mean they've – they've all got different styles of teaching I think – yeah, it's difficult to compare.

Interviewer:	OK, do you find it encouraging having female lecturers? Or would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	Probably. The one that we did have, I mean it was encouraging to see how well she'd done from er the subject in terms of teaching it, and she did have a big influence and I mean it shows that you can get into the industry. But, I mean initially I think it would help but now I don't really – it doesn't bother me as much.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the female lecturers treated you the same as the male lecturers?

Subject:	Treat me?

Interviewer:	Yeah, or female students.

Subject:	Erm, I think some of the male lecturers are more helpful to the girls than to the guys. Female lecturers I think tend to be the same to everyone. But then I think it might be because the girls come across as less confident that the teachers would want to you know, help them more.

Interviewer:	Ok, that's quite interesting, have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	Male.

Interviewer:	And are they approachable or would you rather have a female personal tutor?

Subject:	Erm, he's quite young – I think he's one of the youngest in the department so – and he's quite friendly, so he is approachable but, I mean, I think I'd only go to him with – well, you're only meant to go – I don't know how your meant to use it for personal tutor really, 'cos I don't – we haven't seen him that much (yeah). I said it was a personal problem, I'd probably be put off speaking to him.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anyone else that you could go to for advice on like personal or academic issues or family, if you needed to?

Subject:	I haven't needed to really.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anyone or anything that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the degree?

Subject:	Nothing springs to mind.

Interviewer:	Not anybody?

Subject:	Just like a lecturer or…?

Interviewer:	Well some people have said lecturers, some people have said just having their friends and going to and saying it's motivated them to carry on with their work and things like that.

Subject:	Yeah, I mean on our course everyone's willing to kind of share work and show each other, because it's always – and it's not as though you can copy and I find that quite helpful and encouraging that I can check I'm up to scratch, kind of thing. There's some lecturers whose opinions I value more than others, I suppose, and I – say when we're drawing in class, you'll have the teacher going round making comments and that, that can be motivating. One of my teachers this year, took me aside, at the end of class, and told me that my work didn't come across as confident – confidently enough and just gave me kind of a mini tutorial afterwards and that made me feel a lot better because it was something I was quite worried about before. But other than that there's nothing – nothing major.

Interviewer:	Have you've had to do much group work or presentations?

Subject:	Erm, we've had 2 group projects, which have been quite big and then some group presentations, so far. The group projects – one of them went fine, the other one – me – well me and one member of the group felt that we were putting in a lot more work, which is frustrating – you can't really do anything about it, because they expect you – it's like being in industry, you're meant to sort out your own team problems, but I mean, it has taught me for the future.

Interviewer:	Yes, so you think that there are benefits from group work?

Subject:	Yes, it needs to be done, just not always great to do.

Interviewer:	Were the problems that you had, was that like with men or women or do you think it doesn't play a part in that?

Subject:	It was a guy and a girl so – no, not particularly. I think it depends on the person, whether they're well organised or not.

Interviewer:	Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work then?

Subject:	Yeah, I find that they'll – erm the girls are more conscientious and want to be more organised and planned and have everything set, know exactly what they're doing whereas guys usually just want to get on with it. And er, like last year I had a piece of group work. It was me and 2 boys and they just wanted to get on with it and I'd always think of all the problems, which is probably not always helpful but you need someone who's gonna point that out, and who's gonna think about other issues.

Interviewer:	Do you prefer working with men or women or aren't you bothered?

Subject:	Er, I think I prefer working with men – having said that the – I mean you find that the group if there's a group of girls, they always seem to get the work done before everyone else. (yeah) Or they tend to be more on target. I find that the guys work tends to be better because they're not just – that might just be the level of people on my year.
.
Interviewer:	OK. Do you think there's like any aspects of teaching or advice that you've had that will help you when you're on your placement?

Subject:	Well, all of it, I think.

Interviewer:	What specifically? Do you think that anything from when you did your placement when you was at school will help when you go out into the industry?

Subject:	I hope so. I mean I think that shows you what it's like in a working environment and it gave me a chance to just enter an environment where I didn't know anyone and have to work and get along with everyone and know everyone as well, so that was – I think that will be helpful.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel ready to go on placement now or not?

Subject:	Well, erm, I think work wise I don't feel I'm up to a level where I could work and do my designing for money (yes) but I mean it's meant to be a placement where you learn, so other than that, yes, I do. I feel like I think I would find it fine it's just I don't think my level – the quality of my work is quite good enough to work properly through it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the university could do anything more to help prepare you?

Subject:	Er, we weren't given much help – we haven't been given much help for applying for jobs (right) and I mean I think it's quite a competitive field. My friends, in other universities, on similar courses, have been told – they were told a lot earlier, about the whole process and erm told to start applying to lots of different companies early on. And I'm finding now that I'm ready – I've missed out on quite a few opportunities because a lot of the companies have stopped taking applicants, which is a shame but on the other hand they did tell us that it would be up to us to find a placement and they – they have given us a few emails about companies, but they just haven't given us that much yet.

Interviewer:	OK, do you know where you're going on placement yet?

Subject:	Not yet.

Interviewer:	Why did you decide to do the placement in the end?

Subject:	Because well I'm not ready for third year because I need to have a great idea for a final project and gain confidence about my work. And I'd like to gain some extra knowledge in a year in between. I think it will be good experience, not just work wise but also personally, which is (?) another person and also, I mean there's the more serious things that my parents have told me about – you know – that you generally get higher marks, it kind of gives you the experience already that you'll need later on.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that your parents have been the main influence on making your mind up about going on placement then?

Subject:	Well, also the fact that there were so many people in our year who are doing one, or planning on doing one and I mean they've all come up with similar reasons and plus it makes life as a student a bit longer – just for another year.

Interviewer:	Are there many people on your course not doing a placement?

Subject:	There aren't many people on my course not doing a placement, but then all my friends who aren't on my course are doing 3 year courses, which is a shame.

Interviewer:	OK, what sort of things attracted you to the companies that you've applied to?

Subject:	Erm.

Interviewer:	Have you looked at things like career prospects or training opportunities or the type of work that they're doing?

Subject:	Yeah, it's appealing when they have extra training for you on the software that you're going to need to use and just general things like [company] do a lot of extra training as well as maintenance. And also, I mean when there's a place that's on a team work because it – in general it's better to work as a team (yes) and I think also seeing the product that they've come up with, is important. So I can see the kind of work that they're doing.

Interviewer:	OK, have you done much research into the companies that you've applied to?

Subject:	The company that I've applied to, I've looked at their web pages – I mean I've looked at their portfolio (yes) and for [company] so far we've had a tour of the factory and (been shown?), so that's been helpful.

Interviewer:	OK, what would you have liked the university to do in helping you find a placement?

Subject:	I think if they'd told us, probably last year, to start – I mean we were given a presentation about – from the careers service – about getting a CV ready filling in application forms and things like that. If we'd been told that earlier so that we would have had it ready and we need to get a portfolio ready. I mean we had to use work from the first year for our portfolio and that wasn't – we weren't really told that during first year, and I wish people had kind of said it more so we'd have worked to – so we would have known. Erm, so and told us to get that ready as well, so there was just – we had our CV's and portfolio's and covering letters ready to send off and we had time to look. Or when, as soon as they told us about placements whereas a lot of us didn't have anything until about 4 weeks before Easter, I reckon, which is probably a bit late compared to other universities.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think will be the best and the worst things about going on placement?

Subject:	Erm, the best thing will just be the experience – the new experience for a year in the company and you know, it's kind of a taster for what I want to do for a job, so it's just practice. I don't need to worry too much and just anything that I learn from it. The negative things will be I think if I'm away from university then I'll miss out on the final year of all my other friends and that's probably the only negative thing. Another good thing will be getting some money so I'll be more out of debt.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you think that being at work will differ from being at university?

Subject:	Waking up at the same time everyday. Erm, I think it will be – I'll have more of a routine that's the main thing I notice when I do work during the holidays. It's the routine of getting up, going to work, sitting down and just doing what you need to do. Er, yeah, all of the routine will be different and having free time in the evenings and weekends will be nice. Erm, then also just – I mean I think in businesses they work differently – different to learning - you're actually producing stuff the whole time, so the whole attitude's gonna be different, I think.

Interviewer:	Do you think how you're treated will be different?

Subject:	Well we've been told by some people that – you know – after the first few months, the first few weeks they don't notice you, its fine. I think in big companies you're not going to be noticed as much and you will be treated like the other employees, whereas, in a smaller company, I mean there's always this thing about you know work placement students getting the tea (yeah) things like that, so. I mean there might be, but I don't really mind. I mean I'm not too worried about it, because, at the end of the day, I'm not expecting to be treated like a full employee yet.

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

Subject:	Erm, I don't really know. I'm hoping that my year in industry will help me decide, because there's so many things that we can go into. I mean there's a design consultancy which can be lots of different products or a company that does one specific product, or I mean you can go into packaging or something more engineering and yeah, I'm hoping next year, we'll focus more on the kind of path that I want to take.

Interviewer:	Did you apply to companies now that do a variety of things then?

Subject:	Yeah, I've applied to consultancies and companies that do packaging and companies that are more CAD based – so I mean, I know that I'll enjoy whatever I do and I'll improve skills in that area. I'm just hoping that will help me decide.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think would be your ideal career then?

Subject:	Hmm, I think working in a consultancy appeals to me the most. It's just – I mean eventually I'd like to – I live in London so I'd like to move back there and work in there you know, a fast-paced company with lots of things happening all the time – lots of exciting ideas coming out and getting some money.

Interviewer:	OK, and would you like to go into management?

Subject:	No. Management doesn't really appeal to me – managing other people. I just like being part of the group.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that you'll encounter any difficulties trying to achieve your ideal career?

Subject:	Yes, I mean it's so competitive and I'm not – I don't know I'm particularly ambitious so I probably would be just happy working for a smaller company that's – does one product type. As long as I'm just – I'm enjoying my work and I'm comfortable money wise. So I mean there might be a lack of motivation.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that career prospects are good in design and technology?

Subject:	I think once you've got a foot in the door, yeah and that's why I'm hoping that I'll get a good placement for next year. But, on the other hand, I think – I get the impression that it is very competitive, but coming from [this university] I think you've already got a head start – we've been told because [this university] and [university] are the highest universities for our course, so we should be more highly regarded, from the start.

Interviewer:	OK. Are you happy with all the career choices that you've made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

Subject:	Erm, no. So far it's been fine.

Interviewer:	Good, what 5 words would you use to describe the design and technology industry?

Subject:	Vast, competitive, exciting, mmm

Interviewer:	Would you describe it as masculine?

Subject:	It's not the first thing that comes to my mind, although it is. When I picture a group of designers, I do picture a group of men.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that it will stay like that or do you think that the situation will get better for women in the industry?

Subject:	Erm, I think, from what I've heard there's been more and more females on courses like mine and especially when I went to [university], which is similar to here for the course, they'd had more female interest every year, which they were pleased about 'cos they thought they were cutting off females. So, hopefully, but I think it will probably always have slightly more males in it

Interviewer:	Yes, do you think that any aspect of the culture and characteristics that you've described or the fact that it is masculine, will create any problems for you at all?

Subject:	I hope not. I mean it is a possibility. I hope that employers will see – if they see you as different because I'm female, I hope they'll see that as a good thing rather than a bad thing. (yeah) But I think, you know, probably not the big employers – probably the smaller companies who aren't as up to date as the other ones and will have more – erm, what's the word? – prejudices. Hopefully I won't encounter any.

Interviewer:	OK, that's everything thank you very much. Thanks for your help.

turns.text: Erm, I think it gave me an interest in it, but it was just the fact that I enjoy it and that I'm good at it, that made me choose it really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Did you have any careers advice or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We had Careers Advice at school but I don't think it was that helpful. But I mean it always came up as one of the options that erm I was suited to. You know we went on computer programmes and spoke to advisors.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think it is that appeals to you about the subject?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The subject I'm doing here is so broad, compared to other degrees. You get to do engineering subjects like mechanics and electronics but you get to do – you get to be creative, but you also get to make things as well, which you don't – you don't in many other things so – it's just so broad and varied. I think it's a lot more exciting than sitting, just listening to lots of lectures.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you ever consider doing any other subjects?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I considered doing something more engineering based but I thought that I'd miss the graphics side of it (yes) and I also considered doing the same course but with a language on the side, like French because I did that at A level, but now I'm just doing that on the side here rather than as part of my degree.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how did you decide to come to [this] University?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, I came to the open day, with some friends, and I hadn't expected – I didn't realise they did my subject – well this subject here. So, I went to the product design area – they – the people there – told me that what I wanted to do sounded more like industrial design, which is slightly more creative. So I went on a department tour and picked up the syllabus and it just really appealed to me. It was my favourite course out of all the universities.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you always want to do a sandwich course or did you just like the course and it happened to have…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I didn't. I only changed to that this September (OK). At first I was a bit too scared to go out into industry, in the middle of my degree. I'm still a bit scared I think – it will be really strange but, after advice from my parents I decided to go for it, because I just thought that it adds to your degree and I've been told that you get better marks in the final year, generally and also it will just – in my field you always need a minimum of 1 year's experience, and it'll be an easy way to get that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you decided that you wanted to do design & technology, did you realise it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. I mean I – I was in an all girls school but there were only 6 of us in the whole school who did it at A level and when I went on open days I noticed I was usually one of the only girls. I think here there's more girls than I expected to be. When I went to [name] and some other universities, I saw hardly any other – it was a bit intimidating as well. I was quite scared, especially coming from an all girls environment to suddenly almost the opposite.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that being in an all girls school affected your choice of subjects at all? Do you think you were encouraged more to do maths or science type subjects?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You're encouraged more to do maths and science and IT but – and they weren't going to run design technology for my 'A' levels – for our year, but we did a petition and – I mean I was going to swap schools if they didn't provide it for me because I'd decided that's what I wanted to do. But, it did make me want to be more academic in my choices in general.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Does it ever bother you that there aren't many women on the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, kind of. It's more the fact that it was quite intimidating and I felt – just things like men in the workshops woodwork and things, I just felt as though I would have less background in it because I know it's a stereotypical kind of view that, you know, boys will do that outside of school and I just thought that I'd be further behind and I think boys in general tend to be a lot more confident about their work and it's something that you need to be confident of your own ideas. But I mean, after the first – after the first few months, I realised that I was just on the same level as everyone else really – fine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged to do this sort of subject?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I mean I think the fact that it's male dominated puts off a lot of people because it is quite intimidating and yeah and you kind of – if you don't – I don't know – you might think that you're less likely to get a job in the field, just because it's so male dominated and that people have ideas, even before they meet you because they know you're female. But what I've found is that it's not really the case – well so far.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What do you think could be done to encourage more women to the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, in school – being an all girls' school, it was really – the whole department was not on a level with everything else and I thought a lot of people were put off then. I mean I don't know if they're running A level design technology any more and it's quite disappointing and as I say a lot of people would be really good at it and would really enjoy it. So if they're not getting the chance. So it would be back in school I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that people maybe don't choose to do it because they don't really know what it is about in the first place?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah and also – well, in my case, the GCSE was so much work compared to other subjects. A lot of – finding time to fit it in, which I mean – it's like now, you've still got to put a lot of extra time in and that puts people off 'cos they just think it's gonna take up a lot more time than everything else.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what characteristics do you think make a good designer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: That's hard. Erm, good imagination and confidence in their ideas. You need to be able to communicate your ideas well and verbally and visually. You need to have a good background knowledge of materials and processes, so you know that the product's made and basic mechanics and electronics – so you know a bit of the idea, if possible. I think just erm people usually think it's people here who are more creative, who can draw but it's not just that. It's the ideas we have and how viable they are.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any of those characteristics are more male or more female? I know you said earlier males are probably more confident.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think in general they're a lot more confident when they explain their ideas and show them, whereas when we have girls in the class, they'll explain it but they'll point out the bad bits or they'll apologise and in general the guys don't do that and er the – I think a lot of the girls tend to be neater with their work, rather than just, you know, drawing it and sharing – but on the other hand there's things that girls have, like we keep getting told that females have better appreciation of colour and they're more sensitive to things like shapes and things – which is also useful. I think it's just mainly the confidence thing – the guys tend to be a lot more confident than the girls in their work, and it shows.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, OK. Do you think that there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I think the disadvantage is that in the kind of minority, and people might be put off just because they know – they know so many designers who are good and they're all male. Yeah. But, on the other hand I think it's good to have another point of view, another perspective on things and it's – you know – a slightly different energy in the team – yeah, and maybe a different outlook and different approach, which is more positive.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Has the course been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think so, yeah. I think a lot of people have been surprised and we do have – I think it's a high drop out rate at the beginning, just because the work load is huge compared to well courses like geography, things like that. But, er yeah – it's yeah, it's quite – it's varied and that was what I was looking for.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So were you surprised then at the amount of engineering and technical stuff that there was in it, or were you expecting that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I was hoping it would have as much as it did, last year because I didn't want to kind of lose my knowledge that I'd gained in my A levels, and I still wanted something academic in there, rather than just drawing all day (yes) you know workshop stuff – I wanted to think as well. But I mean I did find some of it quite hard, but they taught it from a basic level, which was quite good so were all on a level with each other by the end of year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did it surprise you that your department is situated in the faculty of social sciences and not say engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I never remember which faculty you're in because I know the course is basically half engineering and half art but I mean they've just – there's a lot of engineering content in it, especially in first year. I mean we're in – we had to walk to the other side of the campus every single day. It belongs a lot more there I think, I mean I don't think – the other subjects that are in social science I think, apart from ergonomics they don't really overlap at all. So…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think has been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, the worst things are the amount of work but then we were told to expect that and the fact that it's a lot of course work, so we have a lot of deadlines in, at the same time, and it's – you don't get much sleep at all. And it – a lot of the work is very time consuming. You can't just – the fact that you – you never actually hand it all in and have no work to do because there's always an on-going project. But then, I suppose that's something that I like anyway. Erm, and the best thing – hmm, I think our department in general, because we have a lot more seminars and workshops. I like the fact that we're a lot more bonded than other courses. We know everyone in the year and we see each other – we can chat during lesson time – it's like school, you can just sit there and work and talk to each other and I really like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think that the number of hours that you have to do will help you when you go to work in the industry because you'll be used to putting in more hours and having more structured?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I mean it's gonna help with me – with my organisation and, at the end of the day, I think I'll be getting a lot more out of my university degree than other people – if you know what – I have a lot more teaching hours so I'm gaining a lot more from the lectures than 3 hours a week.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you pleased that you decided to do this course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yes – still. I've had moments where I've just been overwhelmed by the amount of work, but other than that I do really enjoy it and it is what I want to carry on doing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, erm there aren't as many female lecturers. We had one, Dina, but she's left now. And we had another – visiting lecturer she came in and talked about colour – did some colour workshops. I never really thought about that before. When we go up to engineering we've had female lecturers for materials – other than that they're just mainly male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Erm, have you noticed whether the female and male lecturers have got a different teaching style or whether they teach different types of subjects or anything like that.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, within the department the female teacher – oh we have actually got a couple but I haven't really been taught by them – she was – she focussed a lot more on the emotional side, compared to some of the male lecturers but I mean they've – they've all got different styles of teaching I think – yeah, it's difficult to compare.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you find it encouraging having female lecturers? Or would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably. The one that we did have, I mean it was encouraging to see how well she'd done from er the subject in terms of teaching it, and she did have a big influence and I mean it shows that you can get into the industry. But, I mean initially I think it would help but now I don't really – it doesn't bother me as much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the female lecturers treated you the same as the male lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Treat me?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, or female students.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think some of the male lecturers are more helpful to the girls than to the guys. Female lecturers I think tend to be the same to everyone. But then I think it might be because the girls come across as less confident that the teachers would want to you know, help them more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, that's quite interesting, have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And are they approachable or would you rather have a female personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, he's quite young – I think he's one of the youngest in the department so – and he's quite friendly, so he is approachable but, I mean, I think I'd only go to him with – well, you're only meant to go – I don't know how your meant to use it for personal tutor really, 'cos I don't – we haven't seen him that much (yeah). I said it was a personal problem, I'd probably be put off speaking to him.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is there anyone else that you could go to for advice on like personal or academic issues or family, if you needed to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I haven't needed to really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is there anyone or anything that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the degree?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Nothing springs to mind.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Not anybody?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Just like a lecturer or…?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Well some people have said lecturers, some people have said just having their friends and going to and saying it's motivated them to carry on with their work and things like that.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I mean on our course everyone's willing to kind of share work and show each other, because it's always – and it's not as though you can copy and I find that quite helpful and encouraging that I can check I'm up to scratch, kind of thing. There's some lecturers whose opinions I value more than others, I suppose, and I – say when we're drawing in class, you'll have the teacher going round making comments and that, that can be motivating. One of my teachers this year, took me aside, at the end of class, and told me that my work didn't come across as confident – confidently enough and just gave me kind of a mini tutorial afterwards and that made me feel a lot better because it was something I was quite worried about before. But other than that there's nothing – nothing major.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you've had to do much group work or presentations?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, we've had 2 group projects, which have been quite big and then some group presentations, so far. The group projects – one of them went fine, the other one – me – well me and one member of the group felt that we were putting in a lot more work, which is frustrating – you can't really do anything about it, because they expect you – it's like being in industry, you're meant to sort out your own team problems, but I mean, it has taught me for the future.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, so you think that there are benefits from group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, it needs to be done, just not always great to do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Were the problems that you had, was that like with men or women or do you think it doesn't play a part in that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It was a guy and a girl so – no, not particularly. I think it depends on the person, whether they're well organised or not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I find that they'll – erm the girls are more conscientious and want to be more organised and planned and have everything set, know exactly what they're doing whereas guys usually just want to get on with it. And er, like last year I had a piece of group work. It was me and 2 boys and they just wanted to get on with it and I'd always think of all the problems, which is probably not always helpful but you need someone who's gonna point that out, and who's gonna think about other issues.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you prefer working with men or women or aren't you bothered?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I think I prefer working with men – having said that the – I mean you find that the group if there's a group of girls, they always seem to get the work done before everyone else. (yeah) Or they tend to be more on target. I find that the guys work tends to be better because they're not just – that might just be the level of people on my year. .

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think there's like any aspects of teaching or advice that you've had that will help you when you're on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, all of it, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What specifically? Do you think that anything from when you did your placement when you was at school will help when you go out into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I hope so. I mean I think that shows you what it's like in a working environment and it gave me a chance to just enter an environment where I didn't know anyone and have to work and get along with everyone and know everyone as well, so that was – I think that will be helpful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you feel ready to go on placement now or not?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, erm, I think work wise I don't feel I'm up to a level where I could work and do my designing for money (yes) but I mean it's meant to be a placement where you learn, so other than that, yes, I do. I feel like I think I would find it fine it's just I don't think my level – the quality of my work is quite good enough to work properly through it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the university could do anything more to help prepare you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, we weren't given much help – we haven't been given much help for applying for jobs (right) and I mean I think it's quite a competitive field. My friends, in other universities, on similar courses, have been told – they were told a lot earlier, about the whole process and erm told to start applying to lots of different companies early on. And I'm finding now that I'm ready – I've missed out on quite a few opportunities because a lot of the companies have stopped taking applicants, which is a shame but on the other hand they did tell us that it would be up to us to find a placement and they – they have given us a few emails about companies, but they just haven't given us that much yet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you know where you're going on placement yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not yet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why did you decide to do the placement in the end?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because well I'm not ready for third year because I need to have a great idea for a final project and gain confidence about my work. And I'd like to gain some extra knowledge in a year in between. I think it will be good experience, not just work wise but also personally, which is (?) another person and also, I mean there's the more serious things that my parents have told me about – you know – that you generally get higher marks, it kind of gives you the experience already that you'll need later on.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that your parents have been the main influence on making your mind up about going on placement then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, also the fact that there were so many people in our year who are doing one, or planning on doing one and I mean they've all come up with similar reasons and plus it makes life as a student a bit longer – just for another year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are there many people on your course not doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There aren't many people on my course not doing a placement, but then all my friends who aren't on my course are doing 3 year courses, which is a shame.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what sort of things attracted you to the companies that you've applied to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you looked at things like career prospects or training opportunities or the type of work that they're doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it's appealing when they have extra training for you on the software that you're going to need to use and just general things like [company] do a lot of extra training as well as maintenance. And also, I mean when there's a place that's on a team work because it – in general it's better to work as a team (yes) and I think also seeing the product that they've come up with, is important. So I can see the kind of work that they're doing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you done much research into the companies that you've applied to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The company that I've applied to, I've looked at their web pages – I mean I've looked at their portfolio (yes) and for [company] so far we've had a tour of the factory and (been shown?), so that's been helpful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what would you have liked the university to do in helping you find a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think if they'd told us, probably last year, to start – I mean we were given a presentation about – from the careers service – about getting a CV ready filling in application forms and things like that. If we'd been told that earlier so that we would have had it ready and we need to get a portfolio ready. I mean we had to use work from the first year for our portfolio and that wasn't – we weren't really told that during first year, and I wish people had kind of said it more so we'd have worked to – so we would have known. Erm, so and told us to get that ready as well, so there was just – we had our CV's and portfolio's and covering letters ready to send off and we had time to look. Or when, as soon as they told us about placements whereas a lot of us didn't have anything until about 4 weeks before Easter, I reckon, which is probably a bit late compared to other universities.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think will be the best and the worst things about going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the best thing will just be the experience – the new experience for a year in the company and you know, it's kind of a taster for what I want to do for a job, so it's just practice. I don't need to worry too much and just anything that I learn from it. The negative things will be I think if I'm away from university then I'll miss out on the final year of all my other friends and that's probably the only negative thing. Another good thing will be getting some money so I'll be more out of debt.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you think that being at work will differ from being at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Waking up at the same time everyday. Erm, I think it will be – I'll have more of a routine that's the main thing I notice when I do work during the holidays. It's the routine of getting up, going to work, sitting down and just doing what you need to do. Er, yeah, all of the routine will be different and having free time in the evenings and weekends will be nice. Erm, then also just – I mean I think in businesses they work differently – different to learning - you're actually producing stuff the whole time, so the whole attitude's gonna be different, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think how you're treated will be different?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well we've been told by some people that – you know – after the first few months, the first few weeks they don't notice you, its fine. I think in big companies you're not going to be noticed as much and you will be treated like the other employees, whereas, in a smaller company, I mean there's always this thing about you know work placement students getting the tea (yeah) things like that, so. I mean there might be, but I don't really mind. I mean I'm not too worried about it, because, at the end of the day, I'm not expecting to be treated like a full employee yet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, in terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don't really know. I'm hoping that my year in industry will help me decide, because there's so many things that we can go into. I mean there's a design consultancy which can be lots of different products or a company that does one specific product, or I mean you can go into packaging or something more engineering and yeah, I'm hoping next year, we'll focus more on the kind of path that I want to take.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you apply to companies now that do a variety of things then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I've applied to consultancies and companies that do packaging and companies that are more CAD based – so I mean, I know that I'll enjoy whatever I do and I'll improve skills in that area. I'm just hoping that will help me decide.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think would be your ideal career then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, I think working in a consultancy appeals to me the most. It's just – I mean eventually I'd like to – I live in London so I'd like to move back there and work in there you know, a fast-paced company with lots of things happening all the time – lots of exciting ideas coming out and getting some money.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and would you like to go into management?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. Management doesn't really appeal to me – managing other people. I just like being part of the group.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that you'll encounter any difficulties trying to achieve your ideal career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I mean it's so competitive and I'm not – I don't know I'm particularly ambitious so I probably would be just happy working for a smaller company that's – does one product type. As long as I'm just – I'm enjoying my work and I'm comfortable money wise. So I mean there might be a lack of motivation.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that career prospects are good in design and technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think once you've got a foot in the door, yeah and that's why I'm hoping that I'll get a good placement for next year. But, on the other hand, I think – I get the impression that it is very competitive, but coming from [this university] I think you've already got a head start – we've been told because [this university] and [university] are the highest universities for our course, so we should be more highly regarded, from the start.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Are you happy with all the career choices that you've made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, no. So far it's been fine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Good, what 5 words would you use to describe the design and technology industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Vast, competitive, exciting, mmm

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you describe it as masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It's not the first thing that comes to my mind, although it is. When I picture a group of designers, I do picture a group of men.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that it will stay like that or do you think that the situation will get better for women in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think, from what I've heard there's been more and more females on courses like mine and especially when I went to [university], which is similar to here for the course, they'd had more female interest every year, which they were pleased about 'cos they thought they were cutting off females. So, hopefully, but I think it will probably always have slightly more males in it

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, do you think that any aspect of the culture and characteristics that you've described or the fact that it is masculine, will create any problems for you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I hope not. I mean it is a possibility. I hope that employers will see – if they see you as different because I'm female, I hope they'll see that as a good thing rather than a bad thing. (yeah) But I think, you know, probably not the big employers – probably the smaller companies who aren't as up to date as the other ones and will have more – erm, what's the word? – prejudices. Hopefully I won't encounter any.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's everything thank you very much. Thanks for your help.
